title: Chapter 8: The Full Minute
blurb: Tarrow Dyke have learned to drop the Seven, and Sorrel must choose between the shape she wants and the minute she owes the Breath.

blocks.text: The bait worked exactly as we had drawn it in chalk on Pollard's barn floor. Tarrow's marking Tacker followed Mercy into the cluster at the mouth of their Roost, my six shades closed round the point bird, the seventh shade slid in beside them at my ceiling, and then it was simply not there. Tarrow's Wing had dropped it without looking up from the flock.

I watched my best shape come apart in a single breath. The point bird had been held for perhaps two wingbeats, its seven threads running true to seven shades, and when the seventh went out its thread swung away and found a Ridings bird flying just below, and the point bird slipped loose like a bead off a thread and went back into the body of the flock as if nothing had ever had hold of it. The flock rolled away north-east over the reed, dark and then pale as it turned, a scarf of birds shaken out in the last of the light. Tarrow were one point above us in the table, and they would stay there if this went on.

And a wingspan off my own shade, eighth nearest the point bird, exactly where it had flown at Wenlode and at Ketterby, the forty-first bird flew on, unhurried, its old copper ring catching what light there was.

"Forty," I had said to the Clerk on Wednesday, and Augusta Stannard had smiled at me as though that were the right answer. I had carried that smile for three days, turning it over the way you turn a bird in your hands to find what is wrong with it, and by Friday I had understood it. It was not the smile of someone who believed me. It was the smile a counter must be given on the day she is licensed and swears to write forty: there, now you are one of us. One word had done that. And here was the bird I had told her was not there, so close I could see the worn place on its ring, flying beside my shape while it came apart, and I could not stop counting it. I did not think I ever would.

Tarrow Dyke is a straight cut, older than anyone's grandfather, running between two high grass banks toward the sea, and their Reedbed lies in the wash beside it, reed-poles and flat brown water, with a pumping engine at the south-west end whose chimney stands up over the fen like a finger raised for quiet. When we climbed down from the club bus the redshank went up off the wash crying, and a heron stood in the dyke and did not move for any of us.

The Ringing was in the engine house, among the smell of oil and cold iron. I closed copper on each of them under the great still wheel: Joan 23, Mercy 24, Abel 25, Rhys 26, Lucas 27, and my own 71 last, the band warm from my palm before it touched anyone's skin. I held each wrist a moment after the ring was shut, as I would hold a young bird after ringing it, to let it know nothing worse was coming. Joan took the withy from my hand onto her wrist and said, "Tight enough, is it?" and I said that it was. The counters asked whether any player was sighted and wished to declare it. Nobody spoke. Lucas looked at his hands.

Then the eldest counter drew from the felt bag, and the lot gave Tarrow the north-east Roost to attack, the end the Northing favours, and gave us the south-west, the Roost under the engine chimney. It was luck, and it was not ours. "The Fen's thumb on the scale again," Rhys said, and then a young man from the Levels Courier lifted his camera on the bank and Rhys turned his good side to it without breaking off his sentence.

On Friday the lot at the Circuit Loft had drawn Ridings for this fixture, and the public flight book showed no seven-shade hold entered against Ridings all season, so the flock had never seen the shape. I knew the Ridings birds from three winters of feeding them: steady, slow to startle, birds that would rather go round a thing than over it, and the first of the six to start sitting two by two on the perches when the days drew out.

They paired early here too. All through High Flight I watched them leave us, a pair and then another pair, peeling off the edge and away over the bank toward the sea with their wingbeats matched as if they were one bird drawn twice. I raised two shades for a few minutes to herd, then dropped them to save my call for the Gloaming. Lucas, out by the far Roost with his poles, flinched a beat before my first shade rose, as he always does, and I was glad nobody else on that reed-line had a reason to look at him. When the counters declared roost-light, the counted flock was thirty-four.

I had raised all six again a few minutes before it, with the light gone the colour of weak tea along the bottom of the sky, and Mercy had walked her marker toward our cluster as though she had never had a plan in her life. That was how the Seven went.

After it went I wanted it back so badly that for a breath I thought of building the cluster again. But Tarrow's Wing, a broad woman in an engine-man's jacket with grey hair cut short as a brush, had not once looked at any of us, and anything of hers pulled into a Hobsmere cluster she would drop. The Wenlode Wing had told me the cure himself, kindly, as if he were telling me where the good water was. The Court had let the Seven stand, and a woman at the far end of a reed-line had closed it anyway, simply by refusing to lend me her shade.

So I began to feint. I raised Joan's shade and Abel's low by the Roost mouth in the outline of a cluster, and Tarrow's Callers sent their markers in to stand off it, and I dropped both before anyone came within a pace and raised Rhys's out on the flock's west edge instead, where nobody was watching. Shade up, shade down, the outline of a hold drawn in the air and rubbed out, and between the feints plain herding, shades spread loose along the edge to nudge.

It is slow work, and I loved it. Each time a marker came in to cover a cluster that was not there, Tarrow's ground shape pulled a little out of true, and through the gap I could put a shade on the flock's near edge and bring it a few yards toward us. Rhys ran the west edge with his shade over him and his own voice under it, "And Dorne comes down the line, and the crowd are on their feet," to nobody, to the Courier man, to the reed. The flock came south-west in long slow swings, like water going round in a pan, and every swing brought it a little nearer the engine chimney.
My call had run nineteen minutes unbroken. At twenty the counters would call the Breath.

Tarrow's Wing had been timing my call as any good Wing would, and her Callers were already moving to set their ground for the moment my shades came down. It was the worst minute it could have been. The flock was low over the mouth of Tarrow's Roost, wheeling in the dusk with the light gone thin and grey behind it, and its point bird had four of my shades among its seven and was turned toward the thatch, and I could feel the whole body of the flock on the point of following, the way you feel a door about to give under your hand. With two minutes more I believed I could have put half of them in, or more than half, and left Tarrow nothing.

I knew what skipping was. Overcall: grounded at once, for the rest of the match. And I knew something else, because on Wednesday I had heard Joan read it out word for word to keep me: a Breath skipped, and proved in open Court on a counter's sworn timing, was the one ground written in the charter that would strike a Wing's registration for the rest of the season. Four counters stood at the reed-line with their watches open. There was no fog. There would be nothing to argue.
And I thought of the Clerk's smile in the doorway, and I did not want to give her a reason to smile at me again.
"Breath," the counter called.

I dropped every shade. All six went out over the reed at once, and the point bird's threads swung free and found real birds, and the turned bird was not turned any more. I stood with my hands empty and watched for a full minute while Tarrow's shades came along the edge of the flock, patient and sure, and the flock slid back north-east off the mouth of the Roost, all that slow water I had gathered pouring out of the pan. The wash had gone the colour of pewter, and the dyke beyond the bank lay so still that it held the whole sky upside down, chimney and all. Above the flock the forty-first bird turned once, wide, and kept its distance from everything. I did not look away from any of it.
"Time," said the counter.
I raised all six again. There were five minutes of light left.

I cannot tell those five minutes in good order. I remember the flock splitting, and the sound Joan made when it did. I remember putting every shade I had on the half still over our end, turning its point bird back toward the chimney with the grain, the way the birds already wanted to go to their beds. I remember a few wild starlings coming up out of Tarrow's own reed and joining the flock, as wild birds will. And I remember the dark coming in from the east across the levels like a tide, and the birds pouring down out of it into two Roosts at once.
Full dark. The forty-first bird was gone; I did not see it go. The counters walked out along the reed-line with their lamps.

They counted Tarrow's Roost first, under the chimney. Seventeen. Joan let out a long breath through her teeth: seventeen of thirty-four was half, and half is enough. And there was one more bird, on the lintel above the Roost door, sitting dark against the thatch as if it had not made up its mind.
"Eighteen," Rhys said. "That one's mine. I ran that one in personally. Put that in the Courier."

Two of the counters went up to the door with a lamp. The elder ruled it outside the Roost, on the lintel and not in, and the other agreed; then he lifted the lamp nearer and said it wore no ring at all. A wild bird. It would not have counted wherever it sat. Rhys said that was the cruellest thing that had happened to him all season, and the bird woke and flew off into the dark. I watched the place where it had been: a bird that was there, and that the count did not hold.
They counted our Roost at the north-east end, and Tarrow had seventeen too. Half and half. Two each.

Joan stood in the dark with the withy on her wrist and did her arithmetic out loud, because she always does. "Eighteen to us. Nineteen to Tarrow. One match left, isn't there. Fallowby at home, and Fallowby top of the table, and Tarrow away at Gosmoor." She wiped her face with the back of her hand. "So we beat Fallowby, don't we, and Tarrow drop something at Gosmoor, and we stay up. Anything else and we're down the sump, silt and all."
"Yes," I said, because it was so.

I had called thirty-one minutes, and twenty-one of them were drift-minutes. The pull came on me before the counters had finished cutting the rings, a straight line out over the dyke bank toward the road the Ridings crates would take home to Wenlode. Joan took my hand and walked me along the top of the bank in the dark for twenty-one minutes, swearing the whole way about the state of Tarrow's sluices, and she did not let go.
The club bus came home by the north road, round the far side of the mere, and at the end of the Hobsmere causeway, on Pollard's side, I asked the driver to stop.

The wild roost was down for the night in the reed below his feed shed. I heard it before I could see anything: thousands of starlings settled in the stems and still talking among themselves, a sound like a long sea drawn back over shingle and never quite running out. Beyond them the mere lay black, with a little mist standing on it where the causeway crossed the neck. There was a lamp in the shed. Joan came with me as far as the gate and stopped there.
Pollard was sitting on an upturned feed bin with his hands round a tin mug.
"Two each," I said. "We drew."
He nodded slowly.
I asked him the thing I had come to ask. "Could a Wing skip the Breath to win?"
He did not answer for a long time. The roost talked in the reed. Out on the mere a coot called once and was quiet.

"Wind was south-west, that night," he said at last. "Soft. Bit of mist come up off the mere at roost-light. Like that, there." He moved his mug an inch toward the causeway. "Season one hundred and seventy-four. The cup final. Here, on our Reedbed."
I waited.

"Mist took the far end. Counters lost me past the Roost. Couldn't see the shades to time them." He looked down into his mug. "I knew the minute. I had a watch in my pocket, same as them. Twenty came. I didn't drop."
The roost shifted and muttered in the reed, and settled again.

"We won," he said. "Full settle, last minute of light. Thirty-two minutes I'd held them, unbroken. Somewhere past thirty I couldn't find my own name. I could hear the flock. Every one of them." His voice did not change at all. "Then the dark, and the rings cut, and I was walking. Straight for the neck, there, where the causeway is."
He did not say the next part for a while, and I did not say it for him. Always before I had finished the ends of his thoughts. This one was his, and I let it be.

"My sister had the withy. Edith. She was my tether." He turned the mug round once in his hands. "She got hold of me at the edge, by the causeway stones, and she held me there. Held me a long while. There was ice on the margin, that year." The lamp ticked. "She slipped. I don't know how. She went in, and I was still walking, and when I came back to myself I was on the bank and she wasn't."

The mist stood on the water where the causeway crossed. I looked at it and thought of every time he had met us at this end and come not one step further, and I understood that, and I did not ask about anything else.
"Twenty-nine years," Pollard said.
"I'm sorry," I said. "I'm so sorry."
He nodded, as if that were weather too. Then, very quietly, looking out past the lamp at the mere: "It said something. Past thirty. One word."
I waited. The roost breathed in the reed, thousands of small hearts together in the cold.
"Not tonight," he said.
Joan was waiting at the gate with her collar up and the withy still on her wrist. She did not ask what he had said. She looked at my face and took my arm, and we got back on the bus together.

The bus cannot take the causeway, so it went the long way home round the head of the mere, swaying in the dark, the headlamps finding nothing but reed and the white posts of field gates. Joan sat at the front with Wilfred Cobbing, going over the table in a low voice. Rhys came down the aisle and dropped into the seat beside me.
"Crate," he said. "Here's a thing. The Courier man got my left side. My left side is my second-best side. I'll be in the paper on Tuesday looking like a man who's lost a bet."
I said I thought his left side was good too.

"Kind. Wrong, but kind." He looked at the seat in front of us. "And here's another thing, and you'd better hear it from me. You remember the letter at the Dyke Arms. Grey and gold round the edge. I said it was admirers."
"Yes," I said.

"Well, it was admirers. Paid ones." He smiled his photograph smile. "I've signed a pre-contract with Fallowby Wardens. For next season. If they go up, that's the Sky Division, Crate, proper crowds, and a man who does nothing all day but take photographs. Grey and gold, though. Do you know what grey and gold does for my colouring?" He waited for me to laugh, the way he always waits, with his eyebrows up.
I did not laugh, because it was not funny to me, and there had been a plain question underneath the joke.
"I will miss you on the wing," I said. "You run the west edge better than anyone I have ever seen. I always know where you are without looking."

He opened his mouth to say something quick, and nothing came. He turned his face to the black window, where there was only his own reflection and the reed going by behind it, and for a long while he did not narrate anything at all.
"Don't, Crate," he said at last, very low. "Don't be kind about it. I can manage anything but that."
The bus ground on round the head of the mere. Up at the front Joan said "Fallowby" again, and Wilfred said "Top by a point," and I heard Rhys hear it.
"I'll fly for you on Saturday," he said. "Every yard. You know I will."

I did know it. I also knew what Saturday was: the last day, Hobsmere at home to Fallowby Wardens, the side that top the table by one point, the side that would be his. I would close the copper on his wrist myself at the Ringing, CCIII 26, gently, the way I always close it, and send him out to run the west edge against his own next club with Hobsmere's ring on him.
